metadata.title: Towards Communication Efﬁcient Multi-Agent Cooperations: Reinforcement Learning and LLM
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper proposes a goal-oriented human-interpretable feature communication protocol for multi-robot navigation scenarios, and introduces two frameworks, MAPPO-BDP and LLM-BDP, to optimize feature selection and navigation under bandwidth constraints. The frameworks are shown to effectively complete navigation tasks within a limited number of steps by communicating the most important features under bandwidth constraints.

sections.heading: Cooperations: Reinforcement Learning and LLM
sections.text: Yang Su , Yali Du , Member, IEEE , Yansha Deng , Senior Member, IEEE , and Mischa Dohler , Fellow, IEEE Abstract —Multi-agent systems (MAS) have gained popularity due to their effectiveness in diverse applications. Among these, decentralized approaches, which rely on inter-agent communica- tion, have emerged as a promising alternative to centralized MAS coordination methods. However, existing communication protocols often learn abstract representations that are difficult for humans to interpret. Also, the limited wireless bandwidth in real-world appli- cations imposes a significant challenge on efficient communication among agents. To address these issues, in this paper, we consider a multi-robot navigation scenario and propose a goal-oriented human-interpretable feature communication protocol, enabling robots to transmit only the most semantically important features. Building on this protocol, we first introduce a Multi-Agent Prox- imal Policy Optimization (MAPPO)-based Bandwidth-Adaptive Dual-Policy (MAPPO-BDP) framework, which employs a dual- policy architecture to jointly optimize feature selection and nav- igation under bandwidth constraints. However, as MAPPO-BDP requires retraining for different bandwidth constraints, we fur- ther propose a Large Language Model (LLM)-based Bandwidth- Adaptive Dual-Policy (LLM-BDP) framework. By leveraging LLM-based multi-agents, LLM-BDP can adapt to varying band- width constraints by simply modifying the input prompt, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Experimental results show that both MAPPO-BDP and LLM-BDP frameworks successfully complete navigation tasks within a limited number of steps by ef- fectively communicating the most important features under band- width constraints. We demonstrate that LLM-BDP achieves bet- ter reasoning adaptability by utilizing more advanced LLMs and engineering example prompts. Notably, with human-interpretable feature communication protocol, robots trained with the MAPPO- BDP framework can seamlessly collaborate with robots from the LLM-BDP framework to complete tasks, even without co-training, demonstrating the practical applicability of the proposed commu- nication protocol in new scenarios. sections.heading: IV. LLM-B
sections.text: ASED B ANDWIDTH -A DAPTIVE D UAL -P OLICY F RAMEWORK Our previously proposed MAPPO-BDP framework effec- tively navigates robots to reach landmarks while maintaining communication under constant bandwidth constraints. How- ever, when the bandwidth constraint changes, the MAPPO-BDP framework requires retraining, which is both time-consuming and energy-intensive. To address these issues, we propose an LLM-based Bandwidth-Adaptive Dual policy framework (LLM-BDP), as illustrated in Fig. 3 on the next page. This framework builds upon the goal-oriented human-interpretable feature communication protocol, as detailed in Section II-B , which plays a crucial role in enabling compatibility with LLMs and adaptability to varying bandwidth conditions. Specifically, the protocol encodes robot observations into structured natural- language features that align with LLMs’ text processing capabil- ities. Moreover, bandwidth constraints can be directly provided as part of the prompt input, allowing the system to dynamically adjust communication behaviors without retraining. In the communication phase, we design two LLM-based agents for each robot: the Feature Ranking Agent and the BandwidthAdaptiveAgent.Theseagentsworktogethertodeter- mine which features to broadcast. Notably, when the bandwidth constraint changes, we can simply adjust the prompt input in the Bandwidth Adaptive Agent to meet the updated constraint, eliminating the need for retraining. In the navigation phase, we introduce two additional LLM-based agents: the Navigation Agent and the Collision Avoidance Agent. These agents collab- orate to select appropriate navigation actions, ensuring effective movement while minimizing collision risks. A. Objective Decomposition The overall objective of our system can be divided into two main components: communication and navigation. Each com- ponent has specific goals that are addressed by different agents within the framework. For the communication objective, the goal is to efficiently transmit the most important features within the given bandwidth constraints. This is achieved by two LLM-based agents: the Feature Ranking Agent and the Bandwidth Adaptive Agent. The Feature Ranking Agent evaluates and prioritizes the observed features based on their importance for assisting other robots in achieving their navigation goals and enhancing coordination. The Bandwidth Adaptive Agent then determines how many number of these prioritized features can be transmitted under the current bandwidth conditions. On the other hand, the navigation objective focuses on reach- ing the target landmark as quickly as possible while avoiding collisions. This is managed by the Navigation Agent and the Collision Avoidance Agent. The Navigation Agent identifies the optimal target landmark and generates a set of potential navigation actions to reach it. The Collision Avoidance Agent then assesses these actions for collision risks and selects the safest action to minimize collision risks. B. LLM-Based Agents As shown in Fig. 3 , the LLM-BDP framework leverages specialized LLM-based agents [33] to address the decomposed sub-objectives effectively. Each LLM-based agent incorporates the following components: r TaskSpecification: Eachagentisassignedadetailednatural language description of its task, derived from the corre- sponding sub-objective. For example, the feature-ranking agent receives the following task description: “You are a feature-ranking agent. Your role is to analyze the observed features and assess their importance to other robots.” r Input Format: The input information is transformed into a natural language format to align with the LLM’s capabili- ties. For instance, for the feature-ranking agent, the robot’s local observation ⃗o i t , defined in (8) , is converted into a structured description, such as “At time step t , the robot i observes its velocity v i t , position u i t , and the position of landmark1 ˜ u 1 t and landmark2 ˜ u 2 t ”. r OutputExpectations

sections.text: MAPPO-BDP AND LLM-BDP optimized for efficiency and the latter being the full-scale model with enhanced capabilities. As illustrated in Table III , models in MAPPO-BDP, with significantly fewer parameters compared to gpt-4o and gpt-4o- mini, demonstrate faster inference speeds. However, the primary advantage of GPT models over MAPPO-BDP models lies in their remarkable flexibility. While MAPPO-BDP requires re- training to accommodate varying bandwidth constraints, GPT models can dynamically adapt through prompt modifications, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Additionally, al- though gpt-4o has a slower inference speed than gpt-4o-mini, it delivers significantly greater reasoning capabilities, making it better suited for handling complex tasks. It is worth noting that MAPPO-BDP was trained and tested on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, whereas gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4o were accessed via OpenAI’s API. These comparisons highlight a key trade-off: while GPT- based models provide greater flexibility via prompt-driven con- trol, this comes with higher inference latency and memory usage. Specifically, LLM-BDP incurs additional overhead due to its model size and autoregressive decoding of navigation and communication actions. Although this may limit its real-time ap- plicability, especially in resource-constrained settings, it enables zero-shot adaptation to new goals without retraining. MAPPO- BDP is thus more suitable for latency-sensitive deployments, whereas LLM-BDP fits better in contexts requiring semantic reasoning and generalization. Notably, small-scale LLMs (e.g., 1B–7B parameters) can be deployed on embedded vehicular hardware such as NVIDIA Orin boards [36] and fine-tuned for domain-specific tasks, making on-board LLM-BDP feasible under moderate resource conditions. To further reduce overhead, future work will explore model distillation [37] , edge-cloud co-processing [38] , and the use of smaller domain-specific lan- guage models [39] to mitigate latency and improve the real-time deployability of LLM-BDP. Mischa Dohler (Fellow, IEEE) is currently the VP Emerging Technologies with Ericsson Inc., Silicon Valley, working on cutting-edge topics of 5 G/6 G, AR and Generative AI. He was Professor of wire- less communications with King’s College London, London, U.K., and the Director with the Centre for Telecommunications Research from 2013 to 2021, driving cross-disciplinary research and innovation in technology, sciences and arts. He was also a Senior Researcher with Orange/France Telecom from 2005 to 2008. He is on the Spectrum Advisory Board of Ofcom and on the AI/ML Technical Advisory Committee of the FCC. He is a Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering, Royal Society of Arts, Institution of Engineering and Technology, and a Distinguished member of Harvard Square Leaders Excellence. He is a serial entrepreneur with five companies, composer & pianist with five albums on Spotify/iTunes, and fluent in several languages. He has had ample coverage by national and international press and media, and is featured on Amazon Prime. He is a frequent keynote, panel and tutorial speaker, and has received numerous awards.
